Solomonoff Induction

Cluster D

How an idealized agent should predict. A Bayesian mixture over a countable class of computable hypotheses learns to predict any sequence, with total error bounded by the description length of the truth -- a formal Occam's razor.

By David Quarel (Australian National University), Leon Lang (University of Amsterdam)

What you’ll learn
  • Define the Bayesian mixture over a class of environments and prove it is a proper predictor whose posterior updates multiplicatively.
  • Prove the cumulative prediction-error bound and specialize it to the Solomonoff prior to recover the Occam bound.
  • Show the mixture makes boundedly many mistakes and is Pareto-optimal under KL and squared loss.
  • Bound the misspecified case when the truth lies outside the model class.

Much of this material is drawn from (Hutter et al. 2024, Chapter 3) and the earlier (Hutter 2005); both books provide fuller explanations, additional context, and proofs that we gloss over here.

Difficulty ratings. Each problem is tagged with a rating in square brackets following Knuth's exercise rating scheme~(Knuth 1973): roughly, [00]~trivial, [10]~15--minute pencil-and-paper, [20]~1--2~hours, [30]~several hours to a day, [40]~a significant research result. Intermediate values are possible.

Overview

Solomonoff induction is the prediction half of Universal AI: what would an optimally intelligent agent do if it only had to predict, given unlimited compute and the weakest possible assumptions? The answer is a single Bayesian mixture ξ\xiξ over a countable class M\mathcal{M}M of candidate environments, weighted by a prior wνw_{\nu}wν​. It (eventually) predicts as well as the true environment μ\muμ, and under the universal choice --- M\mathcal{M}M = all computable environments, prior wν=2−K(ν)w_{\nu} = 2^{-K(\nu)}wν​=2−K(ν) with KKK the Kolmogorov complexity --- the assumption $\mu \in \mathcal{M}$'' becomes the universe is computable,'' and Occam's razor drops out of the mathematics.

This module is a worksheet: you build the theory yourself, one problem at a time. The sequel module, AIXI, lifts the same mixture to sequential decision-making (learning to act).

Prerequisites

  • Comfort with discrete probability: conditional distributions, the chain rule, expectations.
  • Kullback--Leibler divergence and basic information theory (helpful, developed as needed).

Goal and Roadmap

A recipe for prediction: Solomonoff induction is an attempt to mathematically formalize the problem of induction from philosophy: How to make predictions about the future based on past observations?

We formalize this as sequence prediction: There is some true environment μ\muμ that generates a sequence x1,x2,…x_{1}, x_{2}, \dotsx1​,x2​,… of (binary) symbols. Each next symbol xt∼μ(⋅∣x<t)x_{t} \sim \mu(\cdot \mid x_{<t})xt​∼μ(⋅∣x<t​) is sampled from μ\muμ conditioned on the past x<tx_{<t}x<t​. A predictor PPP takes the history x<tx_{<t}x<t​ and gives a distribution P(⋅∣x<t)P(\cdot \mid x_{<t})P(⋅∣x<t​) over the next symbol xtx_{t}xt​.

We measure the quality of a predictor PPP by the μ\muμ-expected squared prediction error, summed over every timestep:

S∞μ:=∑t=1∞∑x<t∈B∗μ(x<t)∑xt∈B(P(xt∣x<t)−μ(xt∣x<t))2.\begin{aligned}S_{\infty}^{\mu} := \sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\sum_{x_{<t} \in \mathbb{B}^*}\mu(x_{<t}) \sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\big( P(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) \big)^{2}.\end{aligned}S∞μ​:=t=1∑∞​x<t​∈B∗∑​μ(x<t​)xt​∈B∑​(P(xt​∣x<t​)−μ(xt​∣x<t​))2.​

How to construct a predictor PPP such that S∞μS^{\mu}_{\infty}S∞μ​ is small (or at least finite)? Bayesian inference to the rescue: we choose as our predictor a Bayesian mixture ξ\xiξ over a countable class M={ν1,ν2,… }\Mc = \{\nu_{1}, \nu_{2}, \dots\}M={ν1​,ν2​,…} of candidate environments, weighted by prior beliefs wνw_{\nu}wν​ (formalized in Definition 1.2). The main results we build up to are:

  • Cumulative bound (Section 4): Assuming μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M, S∞μ≤−ln⁡wμS^{\mu}_{\infty} \leq -\ln w_{\mu}S∞μ​≤−lnwμ​. The higher the prior on μ\muμ, the lower the prediction error.
  • Explicit bound (Exercise 4.2): specialize to the Solomonoff prior wν=2−K(ν)w_{\nu} = 2^{-K(\nu)}wν​=2−K(ν) to get S∞μ≤K(μ)ln⁡2S^{\mu}_{\infty} \leq K(\mu)\ln 2S∞μ​≤K(μ)ln2, where KKK is the Kolmogorov complexity.
  • Pareto optimality (Exercise 6.2 and 8.2): no other predictor weakly dominates ξ\xiξ on every ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M, for either KL or squared loss.
  • Misspecified version (Section 7): If μ∉M\mu \not\in \Mcμ∈M, the cumulative bound becomes −ln⁡wμ^+Dn(μ∥μ^)-\ln w_{\hat\mu}+ D_{n}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu)−lnwμ^​​+Dn​(μ∥μ^​): the constant complexity term plus an approximation term Dn(μ∥μ^)=∑t=1ndt(μ∥μ^)D_{n}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} d_{t}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu)Dn​(μ∥μ^​)=∑t=1n​dt​(μ∥μ^​) that in general grows linearly in nnn, so S∞μS^{\mu}_{\infty}S∞μ​ diverges. Here μ^∈M\hat{\mu}\in \Mcμ^​∈M is the ``closest'' environment to μ\muμ.

1. The mixture is a predictor

Definition 1.1 (Environment). An environment ν\nuν assigns to each history x<t∈B∗x_{<t}\in \mathbb{B}^{*}x<t​∈B∗ a predictive distribution ν(⋅∣x<t)∈ΔB\nu(\cdot \mid x_{<t}) \in \Delta \mathbb{B}ν(⋅∣x<t​)∈ΔB over the next symbol. The joint probability of a string is defined by the chain rule

ν(x1:n) := ∏t=1nν(xt∣x<t),ν(ϵ):=1,\nu(x_{1:n}) ~:=~ \prod_{t=1}^{n}\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}), \qquad \nu(\epsilon) := 1,ν(x1:n​) := t=1∏n​ν(xt​∣x<t​),ν(ϵ):=1,

so that ν(x1:t)=ν(x<t)⋅ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:t}) = \nu(x_{<t}) \cdot \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(x1:t​)=ν(x<t​)⋅ν(xt​∣x<t​) and ν(x)=ν(x0)+ν(x1)\nu(x) = \nu(x\texttt{0}) + \nu(x\texttt{1})ν(x)=ν(x0)+ν(x1) for all x∈B∗x \in \mathbb{B}^{*}x∈B∗. The true (unknown) environment generating the data is denoted μ\muμ.

Definition 1.2 (Bayesian mixture ξ\xiξ). Let M={ν1,ν2,… }\Mc = \{\nu_{1}, \nu_{2}, \dots\}M={ν1​,ν2​,…} be a countable class of environments with prior weights wν>0w_{\nu} > 0wν​>0 satisfying ∑ν∈Mwν=1\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu} = 1∑ν∈M​wν​=1. The Bayesian mixture is defined as a prior-weighted mixture over all environments ν\nuν in M\McM:

ξ(x1:t) := ∑ν∈Mwν ν(x1:t).\xi(x_{1:t}) ~:=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{1:t}).ξ(x1:t​) := ν∈M∑​wν​ν(x1:t​).

Its one-step predictive distribution is

ξ(xt∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt∣x<t),\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}),ξ(xt​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​),

with posterior weights

w(ν∣x<t) := wν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t)w(ν∣ϵ):=wν.w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) ~:=~ w_{\nu}\, \frac{\nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}\qquad w(\nu \mid \epsilon) := w_{\nu}.w(ν∣x<t​) := wν​ξ(x<t​)ν(x<t​)​w(ν∣ϵ):=wν​.

Here w(ν∣x<t)w(\nu \mid x_{<t})w(ν∣x<t​) is the posterior belief in ν\nuν after observing x<tx_{<t}x<t​.

The mixture ξ\xiξ is defined as a sum of joint probabilities. To use it as a predictor we need its one-step conditional ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​), and we need to know it is a genuine probability distribution (so that, later, Pinsker's inequality applies to it).

Exercise 1.1 (Generalized chain rule) [05]. The two-term chain rule baked into Definition 1.1 extends to arbitrary contiguous blocks. Show that for any 1≤p≤q≤r1 \leq p \leq q \leq r1≤p≤q≤r and any history x<px_{<p}x<p​ with ν(x<p)>0\nu(x_{<p}) > 0ν(x<p​)>0,

ν(xp:r∣x<p) = ν(xp:q∣x<p)⋅ν(xq+1:r∣x<p xp:q).\nu(x_{p:r}\mid x_{<p}) ~=~ \nu(x_{p:q}\mid x_{<p}) \cdot \nu(x_{q+1:r}\mid x_{<p}\, x_{p:q}).ν(xp:r​∣x<p​) = ν(xp:q​∣x<p​)⋅ν(xq+1:r​∣x<p​xp:q​).
Solution

Expand the conditional as a ratio of joints; the chain rule (Definition 1.1) telescopes the ratio to a product over indices k=p,…,rk = p, \ldots, rk=p,…,r:

ν(xp:r∣x<p) = ν(x1:r)ν(x<p) = ∏k=1rν(xk∣x<k)∏k=1p−1ν(xk∣x<k) = ∏k=prν(xk∣x<k).\nu(x_{p:r}\mid x_{<p}) ~=~ \frac{\nu(x_{1:r})}{\nu(x_{<p})}~=~ \frac{\prod_{k=1}^{r}\nu(x_{k} \mid x_{<k})}{\prod_{k=1}^{p-1}\nu(x_{k} \mid x_{<k})}~=~ \prod_{k=p}^{r}\nu(x_{k} \mid x_{<k}).ν(xp:r​∣x<p​) = ν(x<p​)ν(x1:r​)​ = ∏k=1p−1​ν(xk​∣x<k​)∏k=1r​ν(xk​∣x<k​)​ = k=p∏r​ν(xk​∣x<k​).

For any k≥pk \geq pk≥p, the past x<kx_{<k}x<k​ is just x<px_{<p}x<p​ extended by xp:k−1x_{p:k-1}xp:k−1​, so the same expansion identifies every contiguous sub-block as a conditional with the right history. Splitting the product at index qqq:

ν(xp:r∣x<p) = ∏k=pqν(xk∣x<k)⏟= ν(xp:q ∣ x<p)  ⋅  ∏k=q+1rν(xk∣x<k)⏟= ν(xq+1:r ∣ x<p xp:q).\nu(x_{p:r}\mid x_{<p}) ~=~ \underbrace{\prod_{k=p}^{q} \nu(x_k \mid x_{<k})}_{=\,\nu(x_{p:q}\,\mid\,x_{<p})}\;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{k=q+1}^{r} \nu(x_k \mid x_{<k})}_{=\,\nu(x_{q+1:r}\,\mid\,x_{<p}\, x_{p:q})}.ν(xp:r​∣x<p​) = =ν(xp:q​∣x<p​)k=p∏q​ν(xk​∣x<k​)​​⋅=ν(xq+1:r​∣x<p​xp:q​)k=q+1∏r​ν(xk​∣x<k​)​​.

Exercise 1.2 (Mixture is a predictor) [10]. Starting from ξ(x1:t)=∑ν∈Mwν ν(x1:t)\xi(x_{1:t}) = \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{1:t})ξ(x1:t​)=∑ν∈M​wν​ν(x1:t​), show that

ξ(xt∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt∣x<t),w(ν∣x<t):=wν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t),\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}), \qquad w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) := w_{\nu}\, \frac{\nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})},ξ(xt​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​),w(ν∣x<t​):=wν​ξ(x<t​)ν(x<t​)​,

and conclude that ∑xt∈Bξ(xt∣x<t)=1\sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) = 1∑xt​∈B​ξ(xt​∣x<t​)=1, i.e. ξ(⋅∣x<t)\xi(\cdot \mid x_{<t})ξ(⋅∣x<t​) is a probability distribution over B\mathbb{B}B.

Hint

Write ξ(xt∣x<t)=ξ(x1:t)/ξ(x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) = \xi(x_{1:t}) / \xi(x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​)=ξ(x1:t​)/ξ(x<t​), expand the numerator, and use the chain rule ν(x1:t)=ν(x<t) ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:t}) = \nu(x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(x1:t​)=ν(x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​) (Definition 1.1). For the last part, note that the posterior weights sum to 111.

Solution

The one-step conditional is the ratio of joint to marginal, ξ(xt∣x<t):=ξ(x1:t)/ξ(x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) := \xi(x_{1:t}) / \xi(x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​):=ξ(x1:t​)/ξ(x<t​). Expanding the numerator and applying the chain rule ν(x1:t)=ν(x<t) ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:t}) = \nu(x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(x1:t​)=ν(x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​) to each term:

ξ(xt∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mwν ν(x1:t)ξ(x<t) = ∑ν∈Mwν ν(x<t) ν(xt∣x<t)ξ(x<t) = ∑ν∈Mwν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t)⏟= w(ν∣x<t) ν(xt∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt∣x<t).\begin{aligned}\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) ~&=~ \frac{\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{1:t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}~=~ \frac{\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}\\ ~&=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}\underbrace{\frac{w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}}_{=\, w(\nu \mid x_{<t})}\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}).\end{aligned}ξ(xt​∣x<t​)  ​= ξ(x<t​)∑ν∈M​wν​ν(x1:t​)​ = ξ(x<t​)∑ν∈M​wν​ν(x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​)​= ν∈M∑​=w(ν∣x<t​)ξ(x<t​)wν​ν(x<t​)​​​ν(xt​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​).​

The posterior weights are non-negative and sum to 111:

∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mwν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t) = ξ(x<t)ξ(x<t) = 1.\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \frac{\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}~=~ \frac{\xi(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}~=~ 1.ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​) = ξ(x<t​)∑ν∈M​wν​ν(x<t​)​ = ξ(x<t​)ξ(x<t​)​ = 1.

Therefore ξ(⋅∣x<t)\xi(\cdot \mid x_{<t})ξ(⋅∣x<t​) is a convex combination of the probability distributions ν(⋅∣x<t)\nu(\cdot \mid x_{<t})ν(⋅∣x<t​), so it is itself a probability distribution over B\mathbb{B}B:

∑xt∈Bξ(xt∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t)∑xt∈Bν(xt∣x<t)⏟= 1 = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) = 1.\sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) \underbrace{\sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}} \nu(x_t \mid x_{<t})}_{=\, 1}~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ 1.xt​∈B∑​ξ(xt​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)=1xt​∈B∑​ν(xt​∣x<t​)​​ = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​) = 1.

Exercise 1.3 (Posterior update) [10]. Show that the posterior weight w(⋅∣⋅)w(\cdot \mid \cdot)w(⋅∣⋅) updates multiplicatively as new symbols arrive. For every x1:t∈B∗x_{1:t}\in \mathbb{B}^{*}x1:t​∈B∗ with ξ(x1:t)>0\xi(x_{1:t}) > 0ξ(x1:t​)>0,

w(ν∣x1:t) = w(ν∣x<t)⋅ν(xt∣x<t)ξ(xt∣x<t).w(\nu \mid x_{1:t}) ~=~ w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) \cdot \frac{\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}.w(ν∣x1:t​) = w(ν∣x<t​)⋅ξ(xt​∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​)​.

That is: the new posterior equals the old posterior, scaled by the likelihood ratio of how well ν\nuν predicted the just-observed symbol relative to the mixture's own prediction.

Solution

By Definition 1.2,

w(ν∣x1:t) = wν ν(x1:t)ξ(x1:t),w(ν∣x<t) = wν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t).w(\nu \mid x_{1:t}) ~=~ w_{\nu} \,\frac{\nu(x_{1:t})}{\xi(x_{1:t})}, \qquad w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) ~=~ w_{\nu} \,\frac{\nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}.w(ν∣x1:t​) = wν​ξ(x1:t​)ν(x1:t​)​,w(ν∣x<t​) = wν​ξ(x<t​)ν(x<t​)​.

Apply the chain rule (Definition 1.1) to both ν\nuν and ξ\xiξ: ν(x1:t)=ν(x<t) ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:t}) = \nu(x_{<t})\,\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(x1:t​)=ν(x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​) and ξ(x1:t)=ξ(x<t) ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{1:t}) = \xi(x_{<t})\,\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(x1:t​)=ξ(x<t​)ξ(xt​∣x<t​). Dividing,

w(ν∣x1:t)w(ν∣x<t) = ν(x1:t)ν(x<t)⋅ξ(x<t)ξ(x1:t) = ν(xt∣x<t)ξ(xt∣x<t).\frac{w(\nu \mid x_{1:t})}{w(\nu \mid x_{<t})}~=~ \frac{\nu(x_{1:t})}{\nu(x_{<t})}\cdot \frac{\xi(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{1:t})}~=~ \frac{\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}.w(ν∣x<t​)w(ν∣x1:t​)​ = ν(x<t​)ν(x1:t​)​⋅ξ(x1:t​)ξ(x<t​)​ = ξ(xt​∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​)​.

Rearranging gives the claim.

Exercise 1.4 (Multi-step posterior linearity) [10]. Exercise 1.2 showed that ξ\xiξ's one-step prediction ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​) is the posterior-weighted average of the per-model one-step predictions. The same identity extends to predictions over a whole future segment xt:mx_{t:m}xt:m​: for any t≤mt \leq mt≤m,

ξ(xt:m∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt:m∣x<t).\xi(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}).ξ(xt:m​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt:m​∣x<t​).

That is: the same posterior w(ν∣x<t)w(\nu \mid x_{<t})w(ν∣x<t​) governs ξ\xiξ's predictions for arbitrarily many steps into the future, not just the next one. Show this.

Hint

Write ξ(xt:m∣x<t)=ξ(x1:m)/ξ(x<t)\xi(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}) = \xi(x_{1:m}) / \xi(x_{<t})ξ(xt:m​∣x<t​)=ξ(x1:m​)/ξ(x<t​), expand the numerator using the mixture definition, and apply the generalized chain rule (Exercise 1.1 with p=1p=1p=1, q=t−1q=t-1q=t−1, r=mr=mr=m) to factor each ν(x1:m)=ν(x<t) ν(xt:m∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:m}) = \nu(x_{<t})\,\nu(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t})ν(x1:m​)=ν(x<t​)ν(xt:m​∣x<t​).

Solution

By definition of the conditional and the mixture form ξ(x1:m)=∑νwνν(x1:m)\xi(x_{1:m}) = \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} \nu(x_{1:m})ξ(x1:m​)=∑ν​wν​ν(x1:m​) (Definition 1.2),

ξ(xt:m∣x<t) = ξ(x1:m)ξ(x<t) = ∑νwν ν(x1:m)ξ(x<t).\xi(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \frac{\xi(x_{1:m})}{\xi(x_{<t})}~=~ \frac{\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{1:m})}{\xi(x_{<t})}.ξ(xt:m​∣x<t​) = ξ(x<t​)ξ(x1:m​)​ = ξ(x<t​)∑ν​wν​ν(x1:m​)​.

The generalized chain rule (Exercise 1.1 with p=1p=1p=1, q=t−1q=t-1q=t−1, r=mr=mr=m) gives ν(x1:m)=ν(x<t) ν(xt:m∣x<t)\nu(x_{1:m}) = \nu(x_{<t})\,\nu(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t})ν(x1:m​)=ν(x<t​)ν(xt:m​∣x<t​). Substituting,

ξ(xt:m∣x<t) = ∑νwν ν(x<t)ξ(x<t)⏟= w(ν∣x<t) ν(xt:m∣x<t) = ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt:m∣x<t).\xi(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu} \underbrace{\frac{w_{\nu}\, \nu(x_{<t})}{\xi(x_{<t})}}_{=\, w(\nu \mid x_{<t})}\, \nu(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\, \nu(x_{t:m}\mid x_{<t}).ξ(xt:m​∣x<t​) = ν∑​=w(ν∣x<t​)ξ(x<t​)wν​ν(x<t​)​​​ν(xt:m​∣x<t​) = ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt:m​∣x<t​).

2. KL divergence

The KL divergence between two joint distributions over a length-nnn history splits, by an inductive application of the chain rule for probabilities, into a sum of per-step conditional KLs. This telescoping identity lets us trade a single joint KL over an entire history for a sum of per-step KLs (and vice versa): exactly the bridge we will need in Section 4.

We introduce two pieces of notation that will be used throughout the rest of the worksheet:

Definition 2.1 (Cumulative and per-step KL). For environments / predictors ν,ρ\nu, \rhoν,ρ, horizon n≥1n \geq 1n≥1, and 1≤t≤n1 \leq t \leq n1≤t≤n, the cumulative joint KL and the expected per-step KL at step ttt are

Dn(ν∥ρ) := ∑x1:n∈Bnν(x1:n) ln⁡ν(x1:n)ρ(x1:n),dt(ν∥ρ) := ∑x<t∈Bt−1ν(x<t)∑xt∈Bν(xt∣x<t) ln⁡ν(xt∣x<t)ρ(xt∣x<t),\begin{aligned}D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~&:=~ \sum_{x_{1:n} \in \mathbb{B}^n}\nu(x_{1:n}) \,\ln \frac{\nu(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}, \\[6pt] d_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~&:=~ \sum_{x_{<t} \in \mathbb{B}^{t-1}}\nu(x_{<t}) \sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) \,\ln \frac{\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})}{\rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})},\end{aligned}Dn​(ν∥ρ) dt​(ν∥ρ) ​:= x1:n​∈Bn∑​ν(x1:n​)lnρ(x1:n​)ν(x1:n​)​,:= x<t​∈Bt−1∑​ν(x<t​)xt​∈B∑​ν(xt​∣x<t​)lnρ(xt​∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​)​,​

with the conventions 0ln⁡0q:=00 \ln \tfrac{0}{q}:= 00lnq0​:=0 for q≥0q \geq 0q≥0 and pln⁡p0:=∞p \ln \tfrac{p}{0}:= \inftypln0p​:=∞ for p>0p > 0p>0.

We write D∞(ν∥ρ):=lim⁡t→∞Dt(ν∥ρ)D_{\infty}(\nu \parallel \rho) := \lim_{t \to \infty}D_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho)D∞​(ν∥ρ):=limt→∞​Dt​(ν∥ρ) and D∞μ:=D∞(μ∥ξ)D^{\mu}_{\infty} := D_{\infty}(\mu \parallel \xi)D∞μ​:=D∞​(μ∥ξ).

Theorem 2.2 (KL divergence is non-negative). For any environments ν,ρ\nu, \rhoν,ρ and any horizon n≥1n \geq 1n≥1 and step 1≤t≤n1 \leq t \leq n1≤t≤n:

  • Dn(ν∥ρ)≥0D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) \geq 0Dn​(ν∥ρ)≥0, with equality iff ν(x1:n)=ρ(x1:n)\nu(x_{1:n}) = \rho(x_{1:n})ν(x1:n​)=ρ(x1:n​) for every x1:n∈Bnx_{1:n}\in \mathbb{B}^{n}x1:n​∈Bn with ν(x1:n)>0\nu(x_{1:n}) > 0ν(x1:n​)>0.
  • dt(ν∥ρ)≥0d_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho) \geq 0dt​(ν∥ρ)≥0, with equality iff ν(xt∣x<t)=ρ(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) = \rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(xt​∣x<t​)=ρ(xt​∣x<t​) for every x<tx_{<t}x<t​ with ν(x<t)>0\nu(x_{<t}) > 0ν(x<t​)>0 and every xt∈Bx_{t} \in \mathbb{B}xt​∈B.

Proof in Appendix B.

Exercise 2.1 (Telescoping KL) [10]. Show by induction on nnn that for all environments ν,ρ\nu, \rhoν,ρ,

Dn(ν∥ρ) = ∑t=1ndt(ν∥ρ),D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~=~ \sum_{t=1}^{n}d_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho),Dn​(ν∥ρ) = t=1∑n​dt​(ν∥ρ),

where on the right-hand side, the t=1t=1t=1 summand uses the conventions ν(x1∣x<1):=ν(x1)\nu(x_{1} \mid x_{<1}) := \nu(x_{1})ν(x1​∣x<1​):=ν(x1​), ρ(x1∣x<1):=ρ(x1)\rho(x_{1} \mid x_{<1}) := \rho(x_{1})ρ(x1​∣x<1​):=ρ(x1​).

Hint

For the induction step, factor ν(x1:n)=ν(x<n) ν(xn∣x<n)\nu(x_{1:n}) = \nu(x_{<n})\,\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})ν(x1:n​)=ν(x<n​)ν(xn​∣x<n​) (and likewise for ρ\rhoρ) inside the log; the log splits additively into two pieces matching Dn−1(ν∥ρ)D_{n-1}(\nu \parallel \rho)Dn−1​(ν∥ρ) and dn(ν∥ρ)d_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho)dn​(ν∥ρ).

Solution

By induction on nnn.

Base case (n=1n = 1n=1):

D1(ν∥ρ) = ∑x1ν(x1)ln⁡ν(x1)ρ(x1) = d1(ν∥ρ),D_{1}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~=~ \sum_{x_1}\nu(x_{1}) \ln \frac{\nu(x_{1})}{\rho(x_{1})}~=~ d_{1}(\nu \parallel \rho),D1​(ν∥ρ) = x1​∑​ν(x1​)lnρ(x1​)ν(x1​)​ = d1​(ν∥ρ),

using ν(x1∣x<1):=ν(x1)\nu(x_{1} \mid x_{<1}) := \nu(x_{1})ν(x1​∣x<1​):=ν(x1​) and likewise for ρ\rhoρ.

Induction step. Apply the chain rule for probabilities (Definition 1.1) inside the log: ν(x1:n)=ν(x<n) ν(xn∣x<n)\nu(x_{1:n}) = \nu(x_{<n})\,\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})ν(x1:n​)=ν(x<n​)ν(xn​∣x<n​), and similarly for ρ\rhoρ. The log splits additively:

Dn(ν∥ρ) = ∑x1:n∈Bnν(x1:n) ln⁡ν(x1:n)ρ(x1:n) = ∑x1:nν(xn∣x<n)ν(x<n) ln⁡ν(xn∣x<n) ν(x<n)ρ(xn∣x<n) ρ(x<n) = ∑x1:nν(xn∣x<n)ν(x<n)[ln⁡ν(xn∣x<n)ρ(xn∣x<n) + ln⁡ν(x<n)ρ(x<n)]. = ∑x<nν(x<n)∑xnν(xn∣x<n)ln⁡ν(xn∣x<n)ρ(xn∣x<n)⏟dn(ν∥ρ) + ∑x1:nν(xn∣x<n)ν(x<n)ln⁡ν(x<n)ρ(x<n) = dn(ν∥ρ) + ∑x<nν(x<n)ln⁡ν(x<n)ρ(x<n)⏟Dn−1(ν∥ρ)∑xnν(xn∣x<n) = dn(ν∥ρ)+Dn−1(ν∥ρ) = dn(ν∥ρ)+∑t=1n−1dt(ν∥ρ)=∑t=1ndt(ν∥ρ)\begin{aligned}&D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) \\ ~&=~ \sum_{x_{1:n} \in \mathbb{B}^n}\nu(x_{1:n}) \,\ln \frac{\nu(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}\\ ~&=~ \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n}) \nu(x_{<n}) \,\ln \frac{\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})\,\nu(x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})\,\rho(x_{<n})}\\ ~&=~ \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n}) \nu(x_{<n}) \left[\ln \frac{\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})}~+~ \ln \frac{\nu(x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{<n})}\right]. \\ ~&=~ \underbrace{\sum_{x_{<n}} \nu(x_{<n}) \sum_{x_n} \nu(x_n \mid x_{<n}) \ln \frac{\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{n} \mid x_{<n})} }_{d_n(\nu \parallel \rho)}~+~ \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{n} \mid x_{<n}) \nu(x_{<n}) \ln \frac{\nu(x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{<n})}\\ ~&=~ d_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~+~ \underbrace{\sum_{x_{<n}} \nu(x_{<n}) \ln \frac{\nu(x_{<n})}{\rho(x_{<n})}}_{D_{n-1}(\nu \parallel \rho)}\cancel{\sum_{x_n} \nu(x_n \mid x_{<n})}\\ ~&=~ d_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) + D_{n-1}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~=~ d_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) + \sum_{t=1}^{n-1}d_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho) = \sum_{t=1}^{n}d_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho)\end{aligned}      ​Dn​(ν∥ρ)= x1:n​∈Bn∑​ν(x1:n​)lnρ(x1:n​)ν(x1:n​)​= x1:n​∑​ν(xn​∣x<n​)ν(x<n​)lnρ(xn​∣x<n​)ρ(x<n​)ν(xn​∣x<n​)ν(x<n​)​= x1:n​∑​ν(xn​∣x<n​)ν(x<n​)[lnρ(xn​∣x<n​)ν(xn​∣x<n​)​ + lnρ(x<n​)ν(x<n​)​].= dn​(ν∥ρ)x<n​∑​ν(x<n​)xn​∑​ν(xn​∣x<n​)lnρ(xn​∣x<n​)ν(xn​∣x<n​)​​​ + x1:n​∑​ν(xn​∣x<n​)ν(x<n​)lnρ(x<n​)ν(x<n​)​= dn​(ν∥ρ) + Dn−1​(ν∥ρ)x<n​∑​ν(x<n​)lnρ(x<n​)ν(x<n​)​​​xn​∑​ν(xn​∣x<n​)​= dn​(ν∥ρ)+Dn−1​(ν∥ρ) = dn​(ν∥ρ)+t=1∑n−1​dt​(ν∥ρ)=t=1∑n​dt​(ν∥ρ)​

3. Mixture dominance

The mixture ξ\xiξ never assigns much less probability than any single environment weighted by its prior. This single inequality is the engine behind the cumulative bound of Section 4 below: dividing through gives μ(x)/ξ(x)≤1/wμ\mu(x)/\xi(x) \leq 1/w_{\mu}μ(x)/ξ(x)≤1/wμ​, which is then fed into Pinsker and the chain rule in the proof of the main cumulative bound.

Exercise 3.1 (Mixture dominance) [05]. Show that for every ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M and every x∈B∗x \in \mathbb{B}^{*}x∈B∗,

ξ(x) ≥ wν⋅ν(x).\xi(x) ~\geq~ w_{\nu} \cdot \nu(x).ξ(x) ≥ wν​⋅ν(x).
Solution

By Definition 1.2, ξ(x)=∑ν′∈Mwν′ ν′(x)\xi(x) = \sum_{\nu' \in \Mc}w_{\nu'}\,\nu'(x)ξ(x)=∑ν′∈M​wν′​ν′(x). Every term in this sum is non-negative, so dropping all terms except the one with ν′=ν\nu' = \nuν′=ν can only decrease the sum:

ξ(x) = ∑ν′∈Mwν′ ν′(x) ≥ wν ν(x).\xi(x) ~=~ \sum_{\nu' \in \Mc}w_{\nu'}\, \nu'(x) ~\geq~ w_{\nu}\, \nu(x).ξ(x) = ν′∈M∑​wν′​ν′(x) ≥ wν​ν(x).

Remark (Solomonoff specialization). Under the Solomonoff prior, wν=2−K(ν)w_{\nu} = 2^{-K(\nu)}wν​=2−K(ν), so the bound becomes

ξU(x) ≥ 2−K(ν)⋅ν(x)for every computable ν.\xi_{U}(x) ~\geq~ 2^{-K(\nu)}\cdot \nu(x) \qquad \text{for every computable }\nu.ξU​(x) ≥ 2−K(ν)⋅ν(x)for every computable ν.

This is what makes ξU\xi_{U}ξU​ universal: a single predictor dominates the entire computable model class up to a factor that depends only on the model's description length.

4. Cumulative prediction error bound (main result)

The next ingredient relates squared prediction error to KL divergence~(Cover & Thomas 2006, Lemma~11.6.1). We require the following inequality:

Theorem 4.1 (Pinsker's inequality). Let PPP and QQQ be probability distributions over B={0,1}\mathbb{B}= \{\texttt{0}, \texttt{1}\}B={0,1}, i.e., q0,q1≥0q_{0}, q_{1} \geq 0q0​,q1​≥0 with q0+q1=1q_{0} + q_{1} = 1q0​+q1​=1. Write px=P(x)p_{x} = P(x)px​=P(x) and qx=Q(x)q_{x} = Q(x)qx​=Q(x). Then

∑x∈B(qx−px)2  ≤  ∑x∈Bpxln⁡pxqx.(⋆)\sum_{x \in \mathbb{B}}\big( q_{x} - p_{x} \big)^{2} \;\leq\; \sum_{x \in \mathbb{B}}p_{x} \ln \frac{p_{x}}{q_{x}}. \tag{$\star$}x∈B∑​(qx​−px​)2≤x∈B∑​px​lnqx​px​​.(⋆)

The proof of this inequality is mostly tedious algebra but is included in Appendix A.

Definition 4.2 (Cumulative expected and per step squared prediction error). For environments / predictors ν,ρ\nu, \rhoν,ρ and horizon n≥1n \geq 1n≥1, the cumulative expected squared error and the per-step squared error at step ttt are

Sn(ν∥ρ) := ∑t=1nst(ν∥ρ)st(ν∥ρ) := ∑x<t∈Bt−1ν(x<t)∑xt∈B(ν(xt∣x<t)−ρ(xt∣x<t))2\begin{aligned}\Sn{\nu}{\rho}~&:=~ \sum_{t=1}^{n} s_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho) \\ s_{t}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~&:=~ \sum_{x_{<t} \in \mathbb{B}^{t-1}}\nu(x_{<t}) \sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\bigl(\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})\bigr)^{2}\end{aligned}Sn​(ν∥ρ) st​(ν∥ρ) ​:= t=1∑n​st​(ν∥ρ):= x<t​∈Bt−1∑​ν(x<t​)xt​∈B∑​(ν(xt​∣x<t​)−ρ(xt​∣x<t​))2​

Write S∞(ν∥ρ):=lim⁡n→∞Sn(ν∥ρ)S_{\infty}(\nu \parallel \rho) := \lim_{n \to \infty}\Sn{\nu}{\rho}S∞​(ν∥ρ):=limn→∞​Sn​(ν∥ρ) and S∞μ:=S∞(μ∥ξ)S_{\infty}^{\mu} := S_{\infty}(\mu \parallel \xi)S∞μ​:=S∞​(μ∥ξ).

Exercise 4.1 (Cumulative prediction bound) [15]. Show that

S∞μ≤−ln⁡wμ.S_{\infty}^{\mu}\leq - \ln w_{\mu}.S∞μ​≤−lnwμ​.
Hint

You need Theorem 4.1, Exercise 2.1 and Exercise 3.1.

Solution

The proof is a three-step chain:

S∞μ ≤(1) D∞μ ≤(2) lim⁡n→∞∑x1:nμ(x1:n) ln⁡1wμ =(3) −ln⁡wμ.S^{\mu}_{\infty} ~\stackrel{(1)}{\leq}~ D^{\mu}_{\infty} ~\stackrel{(2)}{\leq}~ \lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{x_{1:n}}\mu(x_{1:n}) \,\ln \tfrac{1}{w_\mu}~\stackrel{(3)}{=}~ -\ln w_{\mu}.S∞μ​ ≤(1)​ D∞μ​ ≤(2)​ n→∞lim​x1:n​∑​μ(x1:n​)lnwμ​1​ =(3) −lnwμ​.

Step (1): Pinsker, pointwise. For each ttt and x<tx_{<t}x<t​, both μ(⋅∣x<t)\mu(\cdot \mid x_{<t})μ(⋅∣x<t​) and ξ(⋅∣x<t)\xi(\cdot \mid x_{<t})ξ(⋅∣x<t​) are probability distributions on B\mathbb{B}B (ξ\xiξ by Section 1), so Theorem 4.1 gives

∑xt(ξ(xt∣x<t)−μ(xt∣x<t))2≤∑xtμ(xt∣x<t) ln⁡μ(xt∣x<t)ξ(xt∣x<t).\sum_{x_t}\bigl(\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})\bigr)^{2} \leq \sum_{x_t}\mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) \,\ln \tfrac{\mu(x_t \mid x_{<t})}{\xi(x_t \mid x_{<t})}.xt​∑​(ξ(xt​∣x<t​)−μ(xt​∣x<t​))2≤xt​∑​μ(xt​∣x<t​)lnξ(xt​∣x<t​)μ(xt​∣x<t​)​.

Multiplying by μ(x<t)≥0\mu(x_{<t}) \geq 0μ(x<t​)≥0 and summing over x<tx_{<t}x<t​ gives st(μ∥ξ)≤dt(μ∥ξ)s_{t}(\mu \parallel \xi) \leq d_{t}(\mu \parallel \xi)st​(μ∥ξ)≤dt​(μ∥ξ), so St(μ∥ξ)≤∑i=1tdi(μ∥ξ)=Dt(μ∥ξ)S_{t}(\mu \parallel \xi) \leq \sum_{i=1}^{t} d_{i}(\mu \parallel \xi) = D_{t}(\mu \parallel \xi)St​(μ∥ξ)≤∑i=1t​di​(μ∥ξ)=Dt​(μ∥ξ) (Exercise 2.1), from which we take t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞.

Step (2): Mixture dominance. By Exercise 3.1, ξ(x1:n)≥wμ μ(x1:n)\xi(x_{1:n}) \geq w_{\mu}\, \mu(x_{1:n})ξ(x1:n​)≥wμ​μ(x1:n​), so μ(x1:n)/ξ(x1:n)≤1/wμ\mu(x_{1:n}) / \xi(x_{1:n}) \leq 1/w_{\mu}μ(x1:n​)/ξ(x1:n​)≤1/wμ​, hence ln⁡(μ/ξ)≤ln⁡(1/wμ)\ln(\mu/\xi) \leq \ln(1/w_{\mu})ln(μ/ξ)≤ln(1/wμ​) pointwise. Substituting into the definition Dn(μ∥ξ)=∑x1:nμ(x1:n)ln⁡(μ/ξ)D_{n}(\mu \parallel \xi) = \sum_{x_{1:n}}\mu(x_{1:n}) \ln(\mu/\xi)Dn​(μ∥ξ)=∑x1:n​​μ(x1:n​)ln(μ/ξ) gives the bound.

Step (3): Total mass. Pull the constant out and use ∑x1:nμ(x1:n)=1\sum_{x_{1:n}}\mu(x_{1:n}) = 1∑x1:n​​μ(x1:n​)=1 (μ\muμ is an environment).

Exercise 4.2 (Explicit complexity bound) [05]. Specialize Section 4 to the Solomonoff prior wν=2−K(ν)w_{\nu} = 2^{-K(\nu)}wν​=2−K(ν) (where K(ν)K(\nu)K(ν) is the length of the shortest program computing ν\nuν) to show

S∞μ≤K(μ)ln⁡2.S_{\infty}^{\mu}\leq K(\mu) \ln 2.S∞μ​≤K(μ)ln2.
Solution

By Section 4, for any prior, S∞μ≤−ln⁡wμS_{\infty}^{\mu}\leq -\ln w_{\mu}S∞μ​≤−lnwμ​. The Solomonoff prior assigns μ\muμ the weight wμ=2−K(μ)w_{\mu} = 2^{-K(\mu)}wμ​=2−K(μ), so

S∞μ ≤ −ln⁡wμ = −ln⁡2−K(μ) = K(μ)ln⁡2.S_{\infty}^{\mu}~\leq~ -\ln w_{\mu} ~=~ -\ln 2^{-K(\mu)}~=~ K(\mu) \ln 2.S∞μ​ ≤ −lnwμ​ = −ln2−K(μ) = K(μ)ln2.

Exercise 4.3 (Per-step error) [05]. Hence prove that the per-step expected prediction error

st:=∑x<t∈Bt−1μ(x<t)∑xt∈B(ξ(xt∣x<t)−μ(xt∣x<t))2s_{t} := \sum_{x_{<t} \in \mathbb{B}^{t-1}}\mu(x_{<t}) \sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\big( \xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) \big)^{2}st​:=x<t​∈Bt−1∑​μ(x<t​)xt​∈B∑​(ξ(xt​∣x<t​)−μ(xt​∣x<t​))2

converges to zero as t→∞t \to \inftyt→∞.

Follows immediately as ∑t=1∞st≤−ln⁡wμ<∞\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} s_{t} \leq -\ln w_{\mu} < \infty∑t=1∞​st​≤−lnwμ​<∞ implies st→0s_{t} \to 0st​→0.

5. Bounded number of prediction mistakes

So far we have bounded squared error. For a deterministic environment (i.e. a single infinite binary sequence x1∗,x2∗,…x_{1}^{*}, x_{2}^{*}, \dotsx1∗​,x2∗​,… in M\McM), one can ask the sharper 0/10/10/1-loss question: how often does the mixture predict the wrong bit? The cumulative bound is strong enough to give an answer.

Let μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M be a deterministic environment, so μ(xt∣x<t)∈{0,1}\mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) \in \{0,1\}μ(xt​∣x<t​)∈{0,1} on every history; write xt∗x_{t}^{*}xt∗​ for the unique bit on which μ(⋅∣x<t∗)\mu(\cdot \mid x^{*}_{<t})μ(⋅∣x<t∗​) puts all its mass. Define the threshold predictor associated with ξ\xiξ: at each step, predict the more-likely bit,

x^t := arg⁡max⁡x∈Bξ(x∣x<t)(break ties arbitrarily).\hat{x}_{t} ~:=~ \arg\max_{x \in \mathbb{B}}\xi(x \mid x_{<t}) \qquad \text{(break ties arbitrarily).}x^t​ := argx∈Bmax​ξ(x∣x<t​)(break ties arbitrarily).

We say the mixture makes a mistake at time ttt if x^t≠xt∗\hat{x}_{t} \neq x_{t}^{*}x^t​=xt∗​.

Exercise 5.1 (Bounded prediction mistakes) [15]. Show that the number of mistakes made by the threshold predictor on the μ\muμ-trajectory is at most

#{ t≥1  :  x^t≠xt∗ } ≤ −2ln⁡wμ.\#\{\, t \geq 1 \;:\; \hat{x}_{t} \neq x_{t}^{*} \,\} ~\leq~ -2 \ln w_{\mu}.#{t≥1:x^t​=xt∗​} ≤ −2lnwμ​.
Hint

At a mistake step, ξ(xt∗∣x<t)≤12\xi(x_{t}^{*} \mid x_{<t}) \leq \tfrac12ξ(xt∗​∣x<t​)≤21​ (why?). The per-step squared error along the deterministic μ\muμ-trajectory simplifies dramatically; bound it from below, then sum.

Solution

Step 1: per-step squared error along the μ\muμ-trajectory. Because μ\muμ is deterministic, the outer sum over x<tx_{<t}x<t​ in dtd_{t}dt​ collapses onto the unique trajectory x<t∗:=x1∗⋯xt−1∗x_{<t}^{*} := x_{1}^{*} \cdots x_{t-1}^{*}x<t∗​:=x1∗​⋯xt−1∗​, with weight μ(x<t∗)=1\mu(x_{<t}^{*}) = 1μ(x<t∗​)=1. Write ξt:=ξ(xt∗∣x<t∗)∈[0,1]\xi_{t} := \xi(x_{t}^{*} \mid x_{<t}^{*}) \in [0,1]ξt​:=ξ(xt∗​∣x<t∗​)∈[0,1] for the mass the mixture places on the correct bit. Since μ\muμ assigns mass 111 to xt∗x_{t}^{*}xt∗​ and 000 to the other bit,

st = ∑xt∈B(ξ(xt∣x<t∗)−μ(xt∣x<t∗))2 = (ξt−1)2+(1−ξt−0)2 = 2(1−ξt)2.s_{t} ~=~ \sum_{x_t \in \mathbb{B}}\big(\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}^{*}) - \mu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}^{*})\big)^{2} ~=~ (\xi_{t} - 1)^{2} + (1 - \xi_{t} - 0)^{2} ~=~ 2(1 - \xi_{t})^{2}.st​ = xt​∈B∑​(ξ(xt​∣x<t∗​)−μ(xt​∣x<t∗​))2 = (ξt​−1)2+(1−ξt​−0)2 = 2(1−ξt​)2.

Step 2: a mistake step contributes at least 12\tfrac1221​. A mistake at time ttt means x^t≠xt∗\hat{x}_{t} \neq x_{t}^{*}x^t​=xt∗​, i.e. the threshold predictor chose the other bit. This requires ξ(x^t∣x<t∗)≥ξ(xt∗∣x<t∗)\xi(\hat{x}_{t} \mid x_{<t}^{*}) \geq \xi(x_{t}^{*} \mid x_{<t}^{*})ξ(x^t​∣x<t∗​)≥ξ(xt∗​∣x<t∗​), i.e. 1−ξt≥ξt1 - \xi_{t} \geq \xi_{t}1−ξt​≥ξt​, i.e. ξt≤12\xi_{t} \leq \tfrac12ξt​≤21​. So at every mistake step,

st = 2(1−ξt)2 ≥ 2⋅14 = 12.s_{t} ~=~ 2(1 - \xi_{t})^{2} ~\geq~ 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{4}~=~ \tfrac12.st​ = 2(1−ξt​)2 ≥ 2⋅41​ = 21​.

Step 3: sum and apply the cumulative bound. Let NNN be the total number of mistakes. Summing dtd_{t}dt​ over mistake steps (non-negative contributions from non-mistake steps only help):

12⋅N ≤ ∑t : x^t≠xt∗st ≤ ∑t=1∞st = S∞μ ≤ −ln⁡wμ,\tfrac12 \cdot N ~\leq~ \sum_{t \,:\, \hat{x}_t \neq x_t^*}s_{t} ~\leq~ \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} s_{t} ~=~ S^{\mu}_{\infty} ~\leq~ -\ln w_{\mu},21​⋅N ≤ t:x^t​=xt∗​∑​st​ ≤ t=1∑∞​st​ = S∞μ​ ≤ −lnwμ​,

where the last step is Section 4. Rearranging, N≤−2ln⁡wμN \leq -2 \ln w_{\mu}N≤−2lnwμ​.

Remark (Solomonoff specialization). Under the Solomonoff prior wμ=2−K(μ)w_{\mu} = 2^{-K(\mu)}wμ​=2−K(μ), so −ln⁡wμ=K(μ)ln⁡2-\ln w_{\mu} = K(\mu)\ln 2−lnwμ​=K(μ)ln2 and the bound becomes

#{ t≥1  :  x^t≠xt∗ } ≤ 2K(μ)ln⁡2.\#\{\, t \geq 1 \;:\; \hat{x}_{t} \neq x_{t}^{*} \,\} ~\leq~ 2 K(\mu) \ln 2.#{t≥1:x^t​=xt∗​} ≤ 2K(μ)ln2.

With ln⁡2≈0.693\ln 2 \approx 0.693ln2≈0.693 the constant is just under 1.41.41.4, so if the true environment μ\muμ is computable, and can be described by a program at most kkk bits long, then the predictor ξ\xiξ will make at worst ≈1.4k\approx 1.4 k≈1.4k mistakes over predicting the entire sequence x1:∞∗x^{*}_{1:\infty}x1:∞∗​. Note that the bound is purely existence-style: it does not say when the mistakes happen. They could all occur at the start, or be arbitrarily far into the future.

6. Pareto optimality under KL loss

The final two sections establish that the Bayesian mixture ξ\xiξ is uniquely Pareto-optimal under both KL and squared prediction loss: no other predictor can do at least as well as ξ\xiξ on every environment ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M without coinciding with ξ\xiξ entirely.

Definition 6.1 (Pareto domination). For some measure of loss F(ν,ρ)\mathcal{F}(\nu, \rho)F(ν,ρ) that takes an environment ν\nuν and a predictor ρ\rhoρ, a predictor ρ\rhoρ weakly Pareto-dominates ξ\xiξ with respect to loss F\mathcal{F}F and class M\mathcal{M}M if

F(ν,ρ) ≤ F(ν,ξ)for every ν∈M.\mathcal{F}(\nu, \rho) ~\leq~ \mathcal{F}(\nu, \xi) \qquad \text{for every }\nu \in \Mc.F(ν,ρ) ≤ F(ν,ξ)for every ν∈M.

ξ\xiξ is Pareto-optimal (w.r.t. F\mathcal{F}F) if the only predictor that weakly dominates it is ξ\xiξ itself.

We specialize F\mathcal{F}F to Dn(ν∥ρ)D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho)Dn​(ν∥ρ) in Section 6 and to Sn(ν∥ρ)\Sn{\nu}{\rho}Sn​(ν∥ρ) in Section 8.

Exercise 6.1 (KL Pythagorean identity) [10]. For any predictor ρ\rhoρ with ρ(x1:n)>0\rho(x_{1:n}) > 0ρ(x1:n​)>0 on every x1:n∈Bnx_{1:n}\in \mathbb{B}^{n}x1:n​∈Bn, show that

Dn(ξ∥ρ) + ∑ν∈Mwν Dn(ν∥ξ) = ∑ν∈Mwν Dn(ν∥ρ).D_{n}(\xi \parallel \rho) ~+~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu} \, D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi) ~=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w_{\nu} \, D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho).Dn​(ξ∥ρ) + ν∈M∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ξ) = ν∈M∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ρ).
Hint

Take the difference between the two summation terms.

Solution

Take the difference ∑νwνDn(ν∥ρ)−∑νwνDn(ν∥ξ)\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) - \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi)∑ν​wν​Dn​(ν∥ρ)−∑ν​wν​Dn​(ν∥ξ). Inside each DnD_{n}Dn​ the ν(x1:n)ln⁡ν(x1:n)\nu(x_{1:n}) \ln \nu(x_{1:n})ν(x1:n​)lnν(x1:n​) pieces cancel, leaving

∑νwνDn(ν∥ρ)−∑νwνDn(ν∥ξ)=∑νwν∑x1:nν(x1:n) [ln⁡ν(x1:n)ρ(x1:n)−ln⁡ν(x1:n)ξ(x1:n)]=∑νwν∑x1:nν(x1:n) ln⁡ξ(x1:n)ρ(x1:n).\begin{aligned}\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) - \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi)&= \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{1:n})\,\Bigl[\ln\tfrac{\nu(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}- \ln\tfrac{\nu(x_{1:n})}{\xi(x_{1:n})}\Bigr] \\&= \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{1:n})\,\ln \tfrac{\xi(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}.\end{aligned}ν∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ρ)−ν∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ξ)​=ν∑​wν​x1:n​∑​ν(x1:n​)[lnρ(x1:n​)ν(x1:n​)​−lnξ(x1:n​)ν(x1:n​)​]=ν∑​wν​x1:n​∑​ν(x1:n​)lnρ(x1:n​)ξ(x1:n​)​.​

The factor ln⁡(ξ/ρ)\ln(\xi/\rho)ln(ξ/ρ) does not depend on ν\nuν, so we swap the order of summation and pull it out, then use ∑νwνν(x1:n)=ξ(x1:n)\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} \nu(x_{1:n}) = \xi(x_{1:n})∑ν​wν​ν(x1:n​)=ξ(x1:n​):

∑νwν∑x1:nν(x1:n) ln⁡ξ(x1:n)ρ(x1:n)=∑x1:nln⁡ξ(x1:n)ρ(x1:n)∑νwνν(x1:n)⏟= ξ(x1:n)=∑x1:nξ(x1:n) ln⁡ξ(x1:n)ρ(x1:n) = Dn(ξ∥ρ).\begin{aligned}\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu} \sum_{x_{1:n}}\nu(x_{1:n})\,\ln \tfrac{\xi(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}&= \sum_{x_{1:n}}\ln \tfrac{\xi(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}\underbrace{\sum_\nu w_\nu \nu(x_{1:n})}_{=\, \xi(x_{1:n})}\\&= \sum_{x_{1:n}}\xi(x_{1:n}) \,\ln \tfrac{\xi(x_{1:n})}{\rho(x_{1:n})}~=~ D_{n}(\xi \parallel \rho).\end{aligned}ν∑​wν​x1:n​∑​ν(x1:n​)lnρ(x1:n​)ξ(x1:n​)​​=x1:n​∑​lnρ(x1:n​)ξ(x1:n​)​=ξ(x1:n​)ν∑​wν​ν(x1:n​)​​=x1:n​∑​ξ(x1:n​)lnρ(x1:n​)ξ(x1:n​)​ = Dn​(ξ∥ρ).​

Rearranging gives the claimed identity.

Exercise 6.2 (KL Pareto-optimality) [05]. Show that ξ\xiξ is Pareto-optimal under Dn(ν∥ρ)D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho)Dn​(ν∥ρ) in the sense of Definition 6.1: if ρ\rhoρ is any predictor with

Dn(ν∥ρ) ≤ Dn(ν∥ξ)for every ν∈M,D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~\leq~ D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi) \qquad \text{for every }\nu \in \Mc,Dn​(ν∥ρ) ≤ Dn​(ν∥ξ)for every ν∈M,

then ρ=ξ\rho = \xiρ=ξ.

Hint

Multiply the assumed inequality by wν≥0w_{\nu} \geq 0wν​≥0 and sum over ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M; then apply the KL Pythagorean identity to recognize the extra non-negative term, which must vanish.

Solution

Multiply the assumed inequality by wν≥0w_{\nu} \geq 0wν​≥0 and sum over ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M:

∑νwν Dn(ν∥ρ) ≤ ∑νwν Dn(ν∥ξ).\sum_{\nu} w_{\nu}\, D_{n}(\nu \parallel \rho) ~\leq~ \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu}\, D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi).ν∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ρ) ≤ ν∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ξ).

The KL Pythagorean identity rewrites the LHS as

Dn(ξ∥ρ)  +  ∑νwν Dn(ν∥ξ),D_{n}(\xi \parallel \rho) \;+\; \sum_{\nu} w_{\nu}\, D_{n}(\nu \parallel \xi),Dn​(ξ∥ρ)+ν∑​wν​Dn​(ν∥ξ),

so Equation 3 forces Dn(ξ∥ρ)≤0D_{n}(\xi \parallel \rho) \leq 0Dn​(ξ∥ρ)≤0. KL is non-negative, hence Dn(ξ∥ρ)=0D_{n}(\xi \parallel \rho) = 0Dn​(ξ∥ρ)=0, which forces ρ(x1:n)=ξ(x1:n)\rho(x_{1:n}) = \xi(x_{1:n})ρ(x1:n​)=ξ(x1:n​) for every x1:n∈Bnx_{1:n}\in \mathbb{B}^{n}x1:n​∈Bn. By chain rule, the conditionals agree at every history x<tx_{<t}x<t​ with ξ(x<t)>0\xi(x_{<t}) > 0ξ(x<t​)>0.

7. Misspecified models: when μ∉M\mu \notin \Mcμ∈/M

The cumulative bound Section 4 assumed the true environment μ\muμ lives in the model class M\McM. What happens when it does not? We now show the bound degrades gracefully: it splits cleanly into a complexity term (cost of not knowing which model is best''), exactly as before, plus a linear-in-time approximation term (cost of no model being right''). See (Hutter 2005, §3.2.8) for the original treatment.

Throughout this section, we no longer assume μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M. We will state the bound in terms of an arbitrary μ^∈M\hat\mu \in \Mcμ^​∈M, so taking the infimum over μ^\hat\muμ^​ on the right-hand side gives the tightest version by using the ``closest'' approximation of μ^∈M\hat{\mu}\in \Mcμ^​∈M to μ\muμ.

Exercise 7.1 (Misspecified KL bound) [10]. Show that for all μ^∈M\hat\mu \in \Mcμ^​∈M,

Dn(μ∥ξ) ≤ −ln⁡wμ^ + Dn(μ∥μ^).D_{n}(\mu \parallel \xi) ~\leq~ -\ln w_{\hat\mu}~+~ D_{n}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu).Dn​(μ∥ξ) ≤ −lnwμ^​​ + Dn​(μ∥μ^​).
Hint

Use Exercise 3.1.

Solution

Mixture dominance applied to μ^∈M\hat\mu \in \Mcμ^​∈M (Section 3) gives ξ(x1:n)≥wμ^ μ^(x1:n)\xi(x_{1:n}) \geq w_{\hat\mu}\, \hat\mu(x_{1:n})ξ(x1:n​)≥wμ^​​μ^​(x1:n​) for every x1:nx_{1:n}x1:n​. Hence μ(x1:n)/ξ(x1:n)≤μ(x1:n)/(wμ^ μ^(x1:n))\mu(x_{1:n}) / \xi(x_{1:n}) \leq \mu(x_{1:n}) / (w_{\hat\mu}\, \hat\mu(x_{1:n}))μ(x1:n​)/ξ(x1:n​)≤μ(x1:n​)/(wμ^​​μ^​(x1:n​)), and taking logs,

ln⁡μ(x1:n)ξ(x1:n) ≤ −ln⁡wμ^  +  ln⁡μ(x1:n)μ^(x1:n).\ln \frac{\mu(x_{1:n})}{\xi(x_{1:n})}~\leq~ -\ln w_{\hat\mu}\;+\; \ln \frac{\mu(x_{1:n})}{\hat\mu(x_{1:n})}.lnξ(x1:n​)μ(x1:n​)​ ≤ −lnwμ^​​+lnμ^​(x1:n​)μ(x1:n​)​.

Now take the μ\muμ-expectation. The LHS becomes Dn(μ∥ξ)D_{n}(\mu \parallel \xi)Dn​(μ∥ξ); the second RHS term becomes Dn(μ∥μ^)D_{n}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu)Dn​(μ∥μ^​); the constant −ln⁡wμ^-\ln w_{\hat\mu}−lnwμ^​​ survives because μ(X1:n)\mu(X_{1:n})μ(X1:n​) has total mass 111.

Remark (Reading the two terms). The right-hand side splits into two qualitatively different terms:

  • −ln⁡wμ^-\ln w_{\hat\mu}−lnwμ^​​ is constant in nnn: under the Solomonoff prior, this is K(μ^)ln⁡2K(\hat\mu)\ln 2K(μ^​)ln2. The familiar ``complexity'' cost of search.
  • The approximation term Dn(μ∥μ^)=∑t=1ndt(μ∥μ^)D_{n}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} d_{t}(\mu \parallel \hat\mu)Dn​(μ∥μ^​)=∑t=1n​dt​(μ∥μ^​) (by Exercise 2.1) is a sum of nnn per-step KLs; in general it grows with nnn. It vanishes identically iff μ^\hat\muμ^​ matches μ\muμ on every μ\muμ-reachable history, in particular when μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M and we pick μ^=μ\hat\mu = \muμ^​=μ, recovering Section 4.

Combining with Pinsker (Theorem 4.1) gives the corresponding bound on S∞μS^{\mu}_{\infty}S∞μ​, which is infinite in general but inherits the rate of μ^\hat\muμ^​.

Details on how to define the best choice of μ^\hat{\mu}μ^​ are in Appendix D.

8. Pareto optimality under squared loss

The squared specialization F(ν,ρ)=Sn(ν∥ρ)\mathcal{F}(\nu, \rho) = \Sn{\nu}{\rho}F(ν,ρ)=Sn​(ν∥ρ) (Definition 4.2) lives one level down from KL: at the conditional distributions ν(⋅∣x<t)\nu(\cdot \mid x_{<t})ν(⋅∣x<t​). The natural Pythagorean decomposition at a fixed history uses posterior weights w(ν∣x<t)w(\nu \mid x_{<t})w(ν∣x<t​): those are the weights that make ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​) the mean of the ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(xt​∣x<t​)'s (via the posterior-predictive form, Definition 1.2). The Pareto-optimality aggregation, however, uses prior weights wνw_{\nu}wν​. Bridging the two takes one extra Bayes-rule step.

Exercise 8.1 (Squared Pythagorean identity) [10]. Fix any t∈{1,…,n}t \in \{1, \dots, n\}t∈{1,…,n} and any history x<t∈Bt−1x_{<t}\in \mathbb{B}^{t-1}x<t​∈Bt−1: the history is arbitrary, not sampled from any environment. For any xt∈Bx_{t} \in \mathbb{B}xt​∈B and any predictor ρ\rhoρ, show

(ξ(xt∣x<t)−ρ(xt∣x<t))2 + ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) (ν(xt∣x<t)−ξ(xt∣x<t))2= ∑ν∈Mw(ν∣x<t) (ν(xt∣x<t)−ρ(xt∣x<t))2.\begin{aligned}&\bigl(\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})\bigr)^{2}~+~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\,\bigl(\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})\bigr)^{2}\\&=~ \sum_{\nu \in \Mc}w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\,\bigl(\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) - \rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})\bigr)^{2}.\end{aligned}​(ξ(xt​∣x<t​)−ρ(xt​∣x<t​))2 + ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)(ν(xt​∣x<t​)−ξ(xt​∣x<t​))2= ν∈M∑​w(ν∣x<t​)(ν(xt​∣x<t​)−ρ(xt​∣x<t​))2.​
Hint

Add and subtract ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​) inside the squared term, then expand. Use ∑νw(ν∣x<t)=1\sum_{\nu} w(\nu \mid x_{<t}) = 1∑ν​w(ν∣x<t​)=1 and the posterior-predictive form of ξ\xiξ (Definition 1.2), ∑νw(ν∣x<t) ν(xt∣x<t)=ξ(xt∣x<t)\sum_{\nu} w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\,\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) = \xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})∑ν​w(ν∣x<t​)ν(xt​∣x<t​)=ξ(xt​∣x<t​), to kill the cross-term. The weighting must be posterior weights w(ν∣x<t)w(\nu \mid x_{<t})w(ν∣x<t​) (not prior weights wνw_{\nu}wν​), because ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ(xt​∣x<t​) is the posterior-weighted mean of the ν(xt∣x<t)\nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν(xt​∣x<t​)'s, not the prior one.

Solution

Throughout, the history x<tx_{<t}x<t​ and symbol xtx_{t}xt​ are fixed but arbitrary. Abbreviate ν:=ν(xt∣x<t)\nu := \nu(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ν:=ν(xt​∣x<t​), ξ:=ξ(xt∣x<t)\xi := \xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ξ:=ξ(xt​∣x<t​), ρ:=ρ(xt∣x<t)\rho := \rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ρ:=ρ(xt​∣x<t​), and w~ν:=w(ν∣x<t)\tilde w_{\nu} := w(\nu \mid x_{<t})w~ν​:=w(ν∣x<t​) for the duration of the calculation.

Step 1: ξ\xiξ is the posterior-weighted mean of the ν\nuν's. By the posterior-predictive form of the mixture (Definition 1.2) and the posterior normalization ∑νw~ν=1\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} = 1∑ν​w~ν​=1,

∑νw~ν ν = ξ.\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} \, \nu ~=~ \xi.ν∑​w~ν​ν = ξ.

Step 2: the cross-term vanishes. A direct consequence of Step 1, again using ∑νw~ν=1\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} = 1∑ν​w~ν​=1:

∑νw~ν (ν−ξ) = ∑νw~ν ν  −  ξ∑νw~ν = ξ−ξ = 0.\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} \, (\nu - \xi) ~=~ \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} \, \nu \;-\; \xi \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} ~=~ \xi - \xi ~=~ 0.ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ξ) = ν∑​w~ν​ν−ξν∑​w~ν​ = ξ−ξ = 0.

Step 3: expand the square. Write ν−ρ=(ν−ξ)+(ξ−ρ)\nu - \rho = (\nu - \xi) + (\xi - \rho)ν−ρ=(ν−ξ)+(ξ−ρ) and expand:

∑νw~ν(ν−ρ)2=∑νw~ν[(ν−ξ)2+2(ν−ξ)(ξ−ρ)+(ξ−ρ)2]=∑νw~ν(ν−ξ)2  +  2(ξ−ρ)∑νw~ν(ν−ξ)  +  (ξ−ρ)2∑νw~ν.\begin{aligned}\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} (\nu - \rho)^{2}&= \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu}\bigl[(\nu - \xi)^{2} + 2(\nu - \xi)(\xi - \rho) + (\xi - \rho)^{2}\bigr] \\&= \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} (\nu - \xi)^{2} \;+\; 2(\xi - \rho)\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} (\nu - \xi) \;+\; (\xi - \rho)^{2} \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu}.\end{aligned}ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ρ)2​=ν∑​w~ν​[(ν−ξ)2+2(ν−ξ)(ξ−ρ)+(ξ−ρ)2]=ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ξ)2+2(ξ−ρ)ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ξ)+(ξ−ρ)2ν∑​w~ν​.​

The middle sum is zero by Step 2; the trailing ∑νw~ν=1\sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} = 1∑ν​w~ν​=1. So

(ξ−ρ)2  +  ∑νw~ν(ν−ξ)2 = ∑νw~ν(ν−ρ)2.(\xi - \rho)^{2} \;+\; \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} (\nu - \xi)^{2} ~=~ \sum_{\nu} \tilde w_{\nu} (\nu - \rho)^{2}.(ξ−ρ)2+ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ξ)2 = ν∑​w~ν​(ν−ρ)2.

Exercise 8.2 (Squared Pareto-optimality) [05]. Show that ξ\xiξ is Pareto-optimal under Sn(ν∥ρ)\Sn{\nu}{\rho}Sn​(ν∥ρ) in the sense of Definition 6.1: if ρ\rhoρ is any predictor with

Sn(ν∥ρ) ≤ Sn(ν∥ξ)for every ν∈M,\Sn{\nu}{\rho}~\leq~ \Sn{\nu}{\xi}\qquad \text{for every }\nu \in \Mc,Sn​(ν∥ρ) ≤ Sn​(ν∥ξ)for every ν∈M,

then ρ(xt∣x<t)=ξ(xt∣x<t)\rho(x_{t} \mid x_{<t}) = \xi(x_{t} \mid x_{<t})ρ(xt​∣x<t​)=ξ(xt​∣x<t​) at every history x<t∈Bt−1x_{<t}\in \mathbb{B}^{t-1}x<t​∈Bt−1 with ξ(x<t)>0\xi(x_{<t}) > 0ξ(x<t​)>0 (equivalently, ξ\xiξ-almost surely) and every xt∈Bx_{t} \in \mathbb{B}xt​∈B. Histories that the mixture never reaches (ξ(x<t)=0\xi(x_{<t}) = 0ξ(x<t​)=0, i.e., reached by no ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M either) are invisible to the loss and are not pinned down.

Hint

Multiply the assumed inequality by wν≥0w_{\nu} \geq 0wν​≥0 and sum over ν\nuν; then for each fixed history x<tx_{<t}x<t​, multiply the per-history Pythagorean identity from above by ξ(x<t)\xi(x_{<t})ξ(x<t​) and use the Bayes identity w(ν∣x<t) ξ(x<t)=wν ν(x<t)w(\nu \mid x_{<t})\,\xi(x_{<t}) = w_{\nu} \,\nu(x_{<t})w(ν∣x<t​)ξ(x<t​)=wν​ν(x<t​) to bridge from posterior weights (inside the identity) to prior weights (in the aggregated Pareto inequality).

Solution

C. Model Class M\McM

All results in this sheet hold for any countable class M\McM and prior wνw_{\nu}wν​. The canonical Solomonoff choice takes M\McM to be the class of all computable environments and the Solomonoff prior

wν := 2−K(ν),w_{\nu} ~:=~ 2^{-K(\nu)},wν​ := 2−K(ν),

where K(ν)K(\nu)K(ν) is the Kolmogorov complexity of ν\nuν: the length of the shortest program that computes ν\nuν. The Bayesian mixture ξ\xiξ under this particular prior is the universal mixture, written ξU\xi_{U}ξU​. With this class the assumption μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M reduces to ``the universe is computable'': as weak an assumption as one can make. For technical details on Kolmogorov complexity, see (Hutter et al. 2024, §2.7).

The class of all computable measures is countable but not enumerable (by the halting problem, you can't decide which Turing machines define total functions), so one can't even formally write ∑ν∈M…\sum_{\nu \in \Mc}\ldots∑ν∈M​… as the decision problem of determining if ν∈?M\nu \overset{?}{\in}\Mcν∈?​M is undecidable. A faithful construction of ξU\xi_{U}ξU​ requires expanding M\McM to all lower-semicomputable semimeasures (Levin), at which point ξU\xi_{U}ξU​ becomes a semimeasure rather than a measure: ∑xξU(x)≤1\sum_{x} \xi_{U}(x) \leq 1∑x​ξU​(x)≤1 instead of =1=1=1, conditionals may not sum to 111, and every other proof in this sheet gains a side-case. This also gives the nice benefit that ξ∈M\xi \in \mathcal{M}ξ∈M.

We dodge all of this: M\McM is just some countable set of proper measures with μ∈M\mu \in \Mcμ∈M, and we assume K(ν)K(\nu)K(ν) is defined for each ν∈M\nu \in \Mcν∈M when we need it. We never need ξ\xiξ itself to be in M\McM, nor do we need its computability, so we don't ask. See (Hutter 2005, §2.4.3) for the full Levin construction.

D. Best choice of μ^∈M\hat{\mu}\in \Mcμ^​∈M.

The bound is valid for every μ^∈M\hat\mu \in \Mcμ^​∈M. A tempting question: which μ^\hat\muμ^​ gives the tightest bound? The answer is genuinely setting-dependent.

Finite horizon nnn. The minimizer of the RHS is

μ^n := arg⁡min⁡ν∈M{−ln⁡wν  +  Dn(μ∥ν)}.\hat\mu_{n} ~:=~ \arg\min_{\nu \in \Mc}\Bigl\{ -\ln w_{\nu} \;+\; D_{n}(\mu \parallel \nu) \Bigr\}.μ^​n​ := argν∈Mmin​{−lnwν​+Dn​(μ∥ν)}.

This is well-defined (finitely many terms, attained when M\McM is finite), but the answer depends on nnn: for small nnn the prior term dominates and a high-prior coarse model wins; for large nnn the fit term dominates and the best per-step approximator wins. Both regimes are correct.

Asymptotic rate. A horizon-free analogue minimizes the per-step KL rate

lim⁡n→∞1n∑t≤ndt(μ∥ν).\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t \leq n}d_{t}(\mu \parallel \nu).n→∞lim​n1​t≤n∑​dt​(μ∥ν).

This is the right notion when one cares about the linear-growth slope of the bound. But it has two drawbacks: the limit need not exist for non-stationary μ\muμ (one can substitute lim inf⁡\liminfliminf but at the cost of clarity), and it discards the prior wνw_{\nu}wν​ entirely, so the minimizer is not the same as μ^n\hat\mu_{n}μ^​n​ at any finite nnn, but only of its slope.

Stationary μ\muμ. The per-step KLs dt(μ∥ν)d_{t}(\mu \parallel \nu)dt​(μ∥ν) are constant in ttt, so all three notions essentially agree: μ^=arg⁡min⁡ν∈MDKL(μ ∥ ν)\hat\mu = \arg\min_{\nu \in \Mc}D_{\text{KL}}(\mu \,\|\, \nu)μ^​=argminν∈M​DKL​(μ∥ν), where the KL is taken under the (common) one-step conditional law. This is the case where ``μ^\hat\muμ^​ = projection of μ\muμ onto M\McM in KL'' has unambiguous meaning.

Upshot. The bound holds for all μ^∈M\hat\mu \in \Mcμ^​∈M, and one is free to take the infimum on the RHS over μ^\hat\muμ^​. Which μ^\hat\muμ^​ actually attains that infimum is a separate question whose answer depends on horizon, prior, and any structural assumptions on μ\muμ.
